name: Nieto Sobejano Arquitectos
bio:
Nieto Sobejano Arquitectos is an architecture practice founded in 1984 by Fuensanta Nieto and Enrique Sobejano, both born in Madrid in 1957, with offices in Madrid and, since 2007, Berlin. The two studied at the Polytechnic University of Madrid and at Columbia University in New York, and both teach. Their work has been shown at the Venice Biennale and the Museum of Modern Art, and the practice has received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture (2010), the European Museum of the Year Award (2012) and the Alvar Aalto Medal (2015). Much of their work adds to historic buildings and sites.

Their major works include the Kunstmuseum Moritzburg extension in Halle, Germany (2008), the Madinat al-Zahra Museum at Córdoba (2009), one of two projects in that city, and the San Telmo Museum extension in San Sebastián (2011); in 2007 the practice received Spain's National Prize for Restoration. The Arvo Pärt Centre at Laulasmaa in Estonia (2018), won in competition in 2014, stays below the canopy of a pine forest except for an observation tower, its glass walls joining an oak-panelled interior to the trees.

name: O'Donnell + Tuomey
bio:
O'Donnell + Tuomey is an Irish architecture practice founded in Dublin in 1988 by the married partners Sheila O'Donnell (born 1953) and John Tuomey (born 1954). Both graduated from University College Dublin in 1976 and then worked in London for James Stirling, O'Donnell on the Clore Gallery at the Tate and Tuomey on the Neue Staatsgalerie in Stuttgart. Back in Dublin they joined Group 91 Architects, which won the competition to regenerate the city's Temple Bar district. Their practice has twice won the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland's Gold Medal, represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2004 and 2008, and is noted, in the words of the Architectural League of New York, "for their expressive form-making".

The Lewis Glucksman Gallery at University College Cork (2004), designed with Arup, was named the best public building in Ireland and shortlisted for the 2005 Stirling Prize. The Lyric Theatre in Belfast (2011) brought them their second RIAI Gold Medal. In London they designed the Saw Swee Hock Student Centre, LSE (2014), and in Budapest the first phase of the Central European University (2016).

name: Peter Celsing
bio:
Peter Celsing (1920–1974) was a Swedish modernist architect who often worked in a brutalist manner, with large surfaces of exposed grey concrete, sometimes set against wide panes of glass that show the structure from outside and interiors finished in wood. Born in Stockholm, he studied at the Royal Institute of Technology and the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts, and was an assistant to Sigurd Lewerentz; according to the architect Adam Caruso, it was Celsing who helped Lewerentz win the competition for St Mark's Church. After a period working in Beirut he led the architecture office of Stockholm's tram and local railway authority, designing suburban metro stations.

His churches include Härlanda Church in Gothenburg (1958). Filmhuset in Stockholm (1971), home of the Swedish Film Institute, was designed to resemble a camera, with a concrete façade like strips of film, and is protected at the highest level by the city museum. Kulturhuset on Sergels torg (1974), a cultural centre meant as an oasis in a rebuilt commercial district, shows a glass front with thin concrete floors like open shelves. Beside it stands the Sveriges Riksbank Building (1976), headquarters of Sweden's central bank.

name: Peter Eisenman
bio:
Peter Eisenman (born 1932) is an American architect and theorist, one of the New York Five and a leading figure of deconstructivism. Born in Newark, New Jersey, he studied at Cornell and Columbia and took a doctorate at the University of Cambridge. He first came to notice with the New York Five, whose members began by reworking the architecture of Le Corbusier. In 1967 he founded the Institute for Architecture and Urban Studies in New York, which he led until 1981. The fragmented forms of his later work placed him in the Museum of Modern Art's "Deconstructivist" exhibition of 1988. He received the Wolf Prize in 2010.

He is known for his numbered houses, among them House VI (Frank Residence) in Cornwall, Connecticut (1975). The Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio (1989) is crossed by a white metal grid like scaffolding and follows two street grids that differ by 12.25 degrees. In Berlin, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe (2005) covers a sloping site with 2,711 concrete stelae of varying heights. His State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona (2006) has a retractable roof.

name: Pierre Jeanneret
bio:
Pierre Jeanneret (1896–1967) was a Swiss architect and designer who worked for about twenty years with his cousin Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, Le Corbusier, and later shaped much of the Indian city of Chandigarh. Born in Geneva, he studied at the city's School of Fine Arts. In 1922 the cousins opened a joint practice in Paris, and from 1927 to 1937 they worked with Charlotte Perriand. Their partnership broke during the Second World War, when Pierre joined the French Resistance while Le Corbusier worked with the Vichy government; they came together again after the war to plan Chandigarh.

The Immeuble Molitor in Paris (1934), an apartment block with façades of glass brick and clear glass, was home to Le Corbusier until his death and is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In Chandigarh, working with Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew, he designed much of the civic architecture and fourteen types of mass housing, and stayed on as the city's chief architect. At Panjab University he designed, with Indian colleagues, the Gandhi Bhawan (1962), surrounded by pools, and the A. C. Joshi Library, Panjab University (1963).

name: Pietro Belluschi
bio:
Pietro Belluschi (1899–1994) was an Italian-American architect, a leading figure of American modernism responsible for more than 1,000 buildings. Born in Ancona, he studied civil engineering in Rome and, from 1923, at Cornell, and then joined the Portland, Oregon, office of A. E. Doyle, where he rose to chief designer and eventually took over the firm. His churches and houses, often in local wood and fitted closely to their sites, helped define a Pacific Northwest regional modernism. From 1951 to 1965 he was dean of architecture and planning at MIT, and in 1972 he received the AIA Gold Medal.

The Equitable Building (Commonwealth Building) in Portland (1948), a concrete-framed office block clad in aluminium, is considered the first office building with a completely sealed, air-conditioned interior, and made his national reputation. In New York he worked with Walter Gropius on the MetLife Building (1963), then the Pan Am Building. 555 California Street in San Francisco (1969), headquarters of the Bank of America, followed, and with Pier Luigi Nervi he designed the city's Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Assumption (1971), whose saddle roof is made of eight hyperbolic paraboloids.

name: Roy Grounds
bio:
Roy Grounds (1905–1981) was an Australian architect based in Melbourne who was often at the forefront of modernism in Victoria. Born in St Kilda, he studied at the University of Melbourne's architectural atelier, worked in London and Los Angeles and returned home in 1932. From 1953 to 1962 he was a partner in the respected firm Grounds, Romberg and Boyd with Frederick Romberg and Robin Boyd. He received the RAIA Gold Medal in 1968 and was knighted in 1969.

In the 1950s he designed houses based on pure geometric shapes; the Roy Grounds House (1953), his own, is a square around a central circular courtyard. His first large commission, the Australian Academy of Science building in Canberra, now called the Shine Dome (1959), is a reinforced concrete dome whose construction was a considerable technical feat. Disagreement with his partners over the National Gallery of Victoria led him to leave the firm and take the commission with him; the gallery opened in 1968, and he gave the next twenty years to the neighbouring Arts Centre Melbourne (1984), which was completed after his death.

name: Rudy Ricciotti
bio:
Rudy Ricciotti (born 1952) is a French architect and publisher known for museums and cultural buildings around the Mediterranean. Born in the Kouba district of Algiers to a family of Italian origin, he moved to France at the age of three, studied engineering in Switzerland and graduated from the school of architecture in Marseille in 1980. He has described himself as opposed to minimalism and speaks in favour of the "demuseumification of museums". He received France's Grand Prix national de l'architecture in 2006, and runs a small publishing house, Al Dante, which publishes photography, writing on architecture and poetry.

The Pavillon Noir in Aix-en-Provence (2006) is among his best-known buildings. He won the competition for the Musée Jean Cocteau, Séverin Wunderman Collection in Menton (2011). The MuCEM in Marseille (2013), the museum of European and Mediterranean civilisations, opened when the city was European Capital of Culture and welcomed 8.5 million visitors in its first three years; France's Court of Audit later criticised its "laborious gestation" and a final cost of €350 million against the €160 million first planned.

name: Sauerbruch Hutton
bio:
Sauerbruch Hutton is an architecture, urban planning and design practice founded in London in 1989 by Matthias Sauerbruch and Louisa Hutton and now based in Berlin, where it is led by the two founders and Juan Lucas Young. Its early commissions in London were small, such as the L House, a Victorian terrace that was the practice's first use of applied colour to make cramped spaces feel larger. Colour as a building material and sustainable design became the two threads of its work, which spans Germany, the United Kingdom, Finland, France, Italy, Switzerland and Luxembourg.

The GSW Headquarters in Berlin (1999), near Checkpoint Charlie, was the first tall building in the city after the fall of the Wall; its one-metre-deep double façade on the west, with coloured blinds, and its "flying roof" ventilate the offices naturally. The German Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt), Dessau (2005), set a benchmark for sustainable office buildings, with a serpentine plan to be experienced on foot. Museum Brandhorst in Munich (2009) is clad in 36,000 vertical ceramic rods in 23 coloured glazes.

name: Sigurd Lewerentz
bio:
Sigurd Lewerentz (1885–1975) was a Swedish architect whose small but exceptional body of work stretches from Nordic Classicism to two late brick churches that still influence architects today. Born at Sandö in Västernorrland, he first trained as a mechanical engineer at Chalmers in Gothenburg, then served an architectural apprenticeship in Germany, and opened his own office in Stockholm in 1911. With Gunnar Asplund he was a main architect of the 1930 Stockholm Exhibition, after which he turned away from architecture for years. He received the Prince Eugen Medal in 1950. The critic James Codrington praised his "daring, often rugged use of materials" and their "indefinable atmosphere".

With Asplund he won the 1914–15 competition for the Woodland Cemetery in Stockholm (1940), though Asplund carried out its later stages alone; he also designed Malmö's Eastern Cemetery. In the last decade of his life two churches revived his career. St. Mark's Church (Markuskyrkan) in Björkhagen, Stockholm (1960), built of brick and timber with small recessed windows, draws on early Christian and Near Eastern brick building. St Peter's Church, Klippan (1966), square in plan, shares the same search for the essential and the primitive.

name: Smiljan Radić
bio:
Smiljan Radić (born 1965) is a Chilean architect based in Santiago who received the Pritzker Prize in 2026. Born in Santiago, he studied architecture at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, graduating in 1989, and then history at the architecture university in Venice. He founded his practice in Santiago in 1995. He often works with his wife, the sculptor Marcela Correa, as on Casa Chica (1997), a tiny house in the Andes. In 2017 he set up the Fundación de Arquitectura Frágil to promote experimental architecture, and in 2026 he shared Chile's National Architecture Award with Alejandro Aravena.

His early work was mostly houses in Chile. The Mestizo Restaurant in Santiago (2007) belongs to the same years, and at Viña Vik Winery in the Millahue valley (2014), designed with Loreto Lyon, he built a winery set into the vineyards. That year he made one of seven bus shelters for the Austrian village project BUS:STOP Krumbach (2014) and the Serpentine Gallery Pavilion in London, a translucent fibreglass shell resting on large quarry stones. The Teatro Regional del Biobío in Concepción (2018) is his largest public building.

name: Thom Mayne
bio:
Thom Mayne (born 1944) is an American architect based in Los Angeles, the founder and principal of Morphosis, who received the Pritzker Prize in 2005. Born in Waterbury, Connecticut, he studied architecture at the University of Southern California and later at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, and first worked as an urban planner. In 1972 he left Cal Poly Pomona with five other students and teachers to found the Southern California Institute of Architecture (SCI-Arc), meant to bring a stronger social conscience to architectural education. He has taught at UCLA, where he held tenure, and at Columbia, Harvard, Yale, the University of Pennsylvania and the Bartlett.

Diamond Ranch High School in Pomona (2000), with Thomas Blurock Architects, sits on a steep hillside once thought unusable. The Caltrans District 7 Headquarters in Los Angeles (2004), a state transport office, was singled out when he received the Pritzker Prize for its environmentally conscious design. 41 Cooper Square in New York (2009), for the Cooper Union, and the Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas (2012), a large cube floating over a landscaped base, followed.

name: Valerio Olgiati
bio:
Valerio Olgiati (born 1958) is a Swiss architect and teacher, trained at ETH Zurich, who calls his approach "non-referential architecture", the title of a 2018 treatise he wrote with the theorist Markus Breitschmid. He has said that moving to Los Angeles mattered more to his formation than his studies, because it taught him to see the world in formal, natural terms rather than symbolic or historical ones. His Iconographic Autobiography (2006), a set of 55 images, sets out the ideas behind his work. He runs his office with his wife Tamara in Portugal and Switzerland, has taught at Harvard, ETH Zurich, Cornell and the Architectural Association, and has been a professor at the Accademia di Architettura in Mendrisio since 2002.

His best-known projects include two early buildings in Switzerland, the Paspels School (1998) and Das Gelbe Haus in Flims (1999), a museum known in English as the Yellow House. The Atelier Bardill in Scharans (2007) followed. His work has been shown at the Royal Institute of British Architects in London and the Colegio de San Ildefonso in Mexico City.

name: WilkinsonEyre
bio:
WilkinsonEyre is an international architecture practice based in London. It began in 1983 as Chris Wilkinson Architects; Jim Eyre became a partner in 1987, and the practice took the name WilkinsonEyre in 1999. It designs bridges as well as large public and cultural buildings, and has won the Stirling Prize. Its work ranges from bridges in Poole, Derry and Stirling to the Wellcome Collection and Stratford station in London, the Mary Rose Museum in Portsmouth, the conversion of Battersea Power Station, and towers in Sydney, Melbourne, Toronto and Guangzhou, where it designed the Guangzhou International Finance Centre.

The Gateshead Millennium Bridge (2001), designed with the engineers Gifford, was the first tilting bridge ever built; its shape and the way it tilts earned it the nickname "Blinking Eye". The Gardens by the Bay Cooled Conservatories in Singapore (2012) include the Flower Dome, the largest glass greenhouse in the world. In Oxford, the Weston Library was named RIBA Building of the Year in 2016. Lille Langebro in Copenhagen (2019), a double-swing bridge, was won in competition with Urban Agency in 2015.

name: Yoshinobu Ashihara
bio:
Yoshinobu Ashihara (1918–2003) was a Japanese architect and writer on cities, best known for the Komazawa Olympic Gymnasium and the Sony Building in Tokyo. He studied at the University of Tokyo and at Harvard, where he took a master's degree in architecture in 1953, and then worked in the practice of the modernist Marcel Breuer. In 1956 he founded his own firm, Yoshinobu Ashihara Architecture Associates, and he later became professor of architecture at the University of Tokyo. He was president of the Japan Institute of Architects from 1980 to 1982 and of the Architectural Institute of Japan from 1985 to 1987, and he received the Order of Culture. His books The Aesthetic Townscape (1979) and The Hidden Order: Tokyo through the Twentieth Century (1986) were translated into English.

For the 1964 Olympics he designed the Komazawa Olympic Park Control Tower and Gymnasium (1964), whose tower became the focal point of the park and whose gymnasium held the wrestling events. The Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre (1990), designed with the acousticians Nagata Acoustics, opened in October 1990, and the Okayama Symphony Hall (1991) followed with the same acoustic consultants.

name: Adolf Loos
bio:
Adolf Loos (1870–1933) was an Austrian and Czechoslovak architect, theorist and polemicist, one of the pioneers of modern architecture and a sharp critic of Art Nouveau. Born in Brno into a family of stonemasons and sculptors, he studied at several schools. His essay Ornament and Crime argued against decoration, in contrast to both the lavish fin-de-siècle style and the Vienna Secession. He developed the Raumplan, or spatial plan, a way of arranging interior rooms on different levels according to their function. He was convicted as a paedophile in 1928, and he died near Vienna in 1933.

His Looshaus on Vienna's Michaelerplatz (1911), built for the tailors Goldman & Salatsch, was attacked in its day for its plain façade, which earned it the nickname "house without eyebrows". The Rufer House in Vienna (1922), a near-cube about 10 metres on each side kept almost bare outside, is considered the first example of the Raumplan. In the Villa Müller in Prague (1930) the Raumplan reaches its fullest form, with rooms set at different heights and lavish interiors of marble, wood and silk behind a plain exterior.

name: Affonso Eduardo Reidy
bio:
Affonso Eduardo Reidy (1909–1964) was a Brazilian modernist architect who shaped some of Rio de Janeiro's best-known public buildings and spaces. The son of an English father and a Brazilian mother, he entered the National School of Fine Arts in Rio at 17, and qualified as an architect in 1930, when Lúcio Costa appointed him teaching assistant to Gregori Warchavchik. He was one of the team, with Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and others, that designed the Ministry of Education and Health in Rio. He worked closely with the engineer Carmen Portinho, his partner, and with the landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx.

The Pedregulho Housing complex (c. 1955), planned in 1946 for lower-paid city employees, stands on the hill that gives it its name and draws on the ideas of Le Corbusier. The Museum of Modern Art, Rio de Janeiro (1967) is a concrete building whose row of external frames, linked by long beams, leaves a gallery floor free of columns. Flamengo Park (1965), which he conceived and designed with gardens by Burle Marx, is the largest public park in Rio and the largest urban seaside park in the world.

name: Aldo Rossi
bio:
Aldo Rossi (1931–1997) was an Italian architect, theorist and designer, one of the leading figures of postmodernism and in 1990 the first Italian to receive the Pritzker Prize. Born in Milan, he studied at the Polytechnic University of Milan, graduating in 1958, and from 1959 helped edit the magazine Casabella-Continuità under Ernesto Nathan Rogers. After working for Ignazio Gardella and Marco Zanuso he turned to teaching, and in 1966 published The Architecture of the City, which became a classic of architectural writing; A Scientific Autobiography followed in 1981. He also designed furniture and objects, including for Alessi. The critic Ada Louise Huxtable called him "a poet who happens to be an architect".

His 1971 competition win for the extension of the San Cataldo Cemetery in Modena (1978) made him internationally famous; it was his largest project and is still unfinished. For the 1980 Venice Biennale he built the floating Teatro del Mondo, a theatre for 250 people. In Maastricht he designed the Bonnefanten Museum (1995), and in Berlin, where he had already built a block on Kochstraße in the 1980s, the Quartier Schützenstraße (1998).

name: Aldo van Eyck
bio:
Aldo van Eyck (1918–1999) was a Dutch architect, one of the most influential figures of Structuralism and a leading voice against the narrow functionalism of post-war modernism. Born in Driebergen, he grew up in England from 1919 and finished school in The Hague before studying at ETH Zurich, graduating in 1942 and staying in Switzerland until the war's end. A member of CIAM, he co-founded Team 10 in 1954 and, with Herman Hertzberger and Jaap Bakema, edited the magazine Forum from 1959 to 1963, calling for a return to humanism in architecture. He taught at the Amsterdam Academy of Architecture and from 1966 to 1984 was a professor at Delft. He often worked with his wife, the architect Hannie van Rooijen, and received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1990 and the Wolf Prize in 1996.

His early work included the plan for the new village of Nagele on the Noordoostpolder and its primary schools. Then came the Amsterdam Orphanage (Burgerweeshuis) (1960), the Pastoor van Arskerk in The Hague (1969), Hubertus House in Amsterdam (1978) and, later, a restaurant and conference centre for the European Space Agency at Noordwijk.

name: Alexander Tamanian
bio:
Alexander Tamanian (1878–1936) was a Russian-born Armenian architect who drew up the first general plan of modern Yerevan and designed many of its principal buildings. Born in Yekaterinodar into a banker's family, he graduated from the St Petersburg Academy of Arts in 1904 and became an Academician of Architecture in 1914. In 1923 he moved to Yerevan to lead building in the new Soviet republic. His plan for the city, approved in 1924, helped turn a small provincial town into a modern capital. His style joined neoclassicism to Armenian traditions, with facings of red tuff and carved stone, and he chaired the committee protecting the country's historic monuments.

The Yerevan Opera Theatre (1953), named after the composer Alexander Spendiaryan, opened in 1933 and was finished in stages. The National Library of Armenia (1939), built to hold some seven million books, reinterprets early and medieval Armenian architecture in what became known as the "Tamanyan style". Government House, Yerevan (1941), on Republic Square, now the seat of the prime minister, earned him a Soviet State Award in 1942, after his death; he is buried in the city's Komitas Pantheon.

name: Ammar Khammash
bio:
Ammar Khammash (born 1960) is a Jordanian architect, designer and artist of Palestinian background whose buildings are rooted in Jordan's landscapes and building traditions. He studied architecture and ethnoarchaeology at the University of Southwestern Louisiana in the United States and began his career with restoration work in Jordan. His projects draw on local craft, ecological and social sustainability and recycled materials, mixing traditional Jordanian building techniques with modern materials. With the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature he restored the abandoned village of Dana and built a guesthouse for the Dana reserve, creating one of Jordan's first eco-tourism sites. He is also a painter, photographer and writer, designed the 4th and 5th series of Jordanian dinar banknotes, and in 2019 received the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture.

His Darat al Funun in Amman (1993) is an arts centre. For the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature he designed the Feynan Ecolodge in Wadi Feynan (2005) and the Royal Academy for Nature Conservation in Ajloun (2014). His Wild Jordan centre in Amman, set into a hillside, won a Guardian-Observer Ethical Travel Award in 2010.

name: Architecture-Studio
bio:
Architecture-Studio is a French architecture practice founded in Paris in 1973 by Martin Robain, who has since been joined by a growing group of partners. It works as a collective, defining architecture as "an art that is socially committed and engaged in the construction of mankind's living environment" and developing each design through team debate rather than individual authorship. With Jean Nouvel it designed the Arab World Institute in Paris, and after the 2001 Shanghai exposition it began to grow in China, where it has an office in Shanghai; it also runs a research centre, CA'ASI, in Venice.

The Notre-Dame-de-l'Arche-d'Alliance in Paris (1998), a Catholic church, is a perfect cube 18 metres on each side wrapped in a stainless-steel framework that glows at night, beside a bell tower like a slender steel lance. The Louise Weiss Building, European Parliament in Strasbourg (1999), won in an international competition in 1991, is the Parliament's principal building, with 220,000 square metres of floor and a distinctive 60-metre tower. In Athens the practice won the competition for Onassis Stegi (2010), a cultural centre on Syngrou Avenue with halls for 900 and 200 people.

name: Aris Konstantinidis
bio:
Aris Konstantinidis (1913–1993) was a Greek modernist architect whose work, rooted in the country's anonymous vernacular building and its landscape, laid the ground for a modern Greek architecture. Born in Athens, he studied at the Technical University of Munich from 1931 to 1936, where he met the Modern Movement, and then worked for the town planning department of Athens and the Ministry of Public Works. He led the Workers' Housing Organisation from 1955 to 1975 and, from 1957 to 1967, the technical service of the Greek National Tourism Organisation, planning workers' housing across the country and the state-built Xenia hotels. His books on Greek vernacular architecture, argued that tradition and landscape should ground modern practice. In the 1980s Alexander Tzonis, Liane Lefaivre and Kenneth Frampton linked his work to critical regionalism.

The Weekend House, Anavyssos (1962) is the most emblematic of his private projects. For the tourism organisation he designed the Xenia Hotel, Mykonos (1960), one of a series of state hotels that also included Kalambaka and Olympia. The Archaeological Museum of Ioannina (1966) is among his public museums, alongside the museum at Komotini.

name: Arup
bio:
Arup is a British multinational firm of engineers, designers, architects and planners, with about 17,000 staff in more than 90 offices in 35 countries. It was founded in London in 1946 by Ove Arup, an expert in reinforced concrete who had engineered Lubetkin's Penguin Pool at London Zoo, as a group of many disciplines working together, an idea he called "Total Design", meant to serve peace and social progress after the war. His work as lead engineer on the Sydney Opera House made the firm famous for complex projects. Arup stepped back in 1970, and the firm is owned in trust for its employees.

Arup engineered many landmarks designed by others, from the Centre Pompidou to the Beijing National Stadium. With Foster + Partners, NACO and the Beijing Institute of Architectural Design it designed Beijing Capital International Airport Terminal 3 (2008), at its opening the largest airport terminal in the world by floor area. With Cox Architecture it designed two bridges: the Kurilpa Bridge in Brisbane (2009), the world's largest hybrid tensegrity bridge, and the Helix Bridge in Singapore (2010), a footbridge shaped like a strand of DNA.

name: Basil Spence
bio:
Basil Spence (1907–1976) was a Scottish architect best known for Coventry Cathedral and for the Beehive in Wellington, New Zealand, and the designer of many other buildings in a modernist and brutalist manner. Born in Bombay, he was sent to school in Edinburgh and studied architecture at Edinburgh College of Art. In 1929–30 he worked in the London office of Sir Edwin Lutyens on designs for the Viceroy's House in New Delhi, a lasting influence on his style. He was President of the Royal Institute of British Architects from 1958 to 1960 and was knighted in 1960 for his work at Coventry.

The old cathedral at Coventry was destroyed by German bombing in 1940, and in 1950 Spence won the competition for its replacement. Coventry Cathedral (1962) stands beside the ruins and tower of the old one, the two together a symbol of wartime destruction and of reconciliation. The Mortonhall Crematorium in Edinburgh (1967), is an example of his post-war expressionist style and is listed Category A. In the 1960s he made the concept design for the Beehive (1981), the executive wing of New Zealand's Parliament, completed after his death.

name: Benedetta Tagliabue
bio:
Benedetta Tagliabue (born 1963) is an Italian architect based in Barcelona, principal and director of the studio Miralles Tagliabue EMBT, which she founded with her husband, the Spanish architect Enric Miralles. Born in Milan, she grew up between Italy and Spain, studied at the Università Iuav di Venezia, graduating in 1989, and worked in New York with Agrest and Gandelsonas. In 1994 she and Miralles formed EMBT in Barcelona, which a year later won Spain's National Architecture Award for a boarding school in Morella. After Miralles died in 2000 she completed his largest projects and went on to lead the studio, whose later work includes the Spanish Pavilion at the 2010 Shanghai Expo. She teaches at the Barcelona School of Architecture and is president of the Enric Miralles Foundation, a research centre in his honour.

The Scottish Parliament Building in Edinburgh (2004), which she saw through to completion, won the 2005 Stirling Prize. In Barcelona she completed the remodelling of the Santa Caterina Market (2005) and the Gas Natural Building (2005), a tower whose glazed blocks cantilever out from its side.

name: Bernard Tschumi
bio:
Bernard Tschumi (born 1944) is an architect, writer and teacher associated with deconstructivism, a French and Swiss citizen who works in New York and Paris. Born in Lausanne, the son of the Swiss architect Jean Tschumi, he studied in Paris and at ETH Zurich, graduating in 1969, and made his name first as a theorist. Projects such as The Manhattan Transcripts (1981) borrowed montage from film to argue that there is no fixed relationship between an architectural form and the events that take place in it. From 1988 to 2003 he was dean of Columbia University's architecture school, and in 1996 he received France's Grand Prix national de l'architecture.

His winning entry in the competition for the 55-hectare parc de la Villette in Paris (1987) became his first major public work. Le Fresnoy in Tourcoing (1997), a national studio for contemporary arts, sets a huge umbrella roof over older buildings, creating a zone of ramps and catwalks between them. The Acropolis Museum in Athens (2009) stands over an archaeological site, with glass floors showing the excavations, and its glass-walled top-floor hall repeats the column spacing of the Parthenon itself.

facts.claim: Born 25 January 1944 in Lausanne; architect, writer and educator associated with deconstructivism; son of Jean Tschumi; dual French-Swiss national; works in New York and Paris; studied in Paris and at ETH Zurich, degree 1969; taught at the AA, IAUS, Princeton, Cooper Union; Dean of Columbia GSAPP 1988–2003; Grand Prix National d'Architecture 1996

Built his reputation as a theorist through writings and drawings; The Screenplays (1977) and The Manhattan Transcripts (1981), montage techniques from film; no fixed relationship between architectural form and the events within it; winning entry for the 1982 55-hectare Parc de la Villette competition his first major public work
facts.note: the article dates the Villette competition to both 1982 and 1983

facts.claim: Le Fresnoy, Studio National des Arts Contemporains, Tourcoing: designed 1992, completed 1999; huge umbrella roof above existing buildings creating a zone of ramps and catwalks
facts.note: the article says Le Fresnoy was completed in 1999; the wall gives 1997

facts.claim: Acropolis Museum: opened 20 June 2009; built over an archaeological site, with glass floors showing the excavations; Parthenon hall with the same column spacing as the temple and glass walls

name: Brinkman & Van der Vlugt
bio:
Brinkman & Van der Vlugt was a Rotterdam architecture practice of the Dutch modern movement, the Nieuwe Bouwen. When the Rotterdam architect Michiel Brinkman died in 1925, his son Johannes Brinkman (1902–1949), a civil engineer, took over the office and made the architect Leendert van der Vlugt (1894–1936) his partner. The partnership lasted only about ten years, until Van der Vlugt died of Hodgkin's disease in 1936. Credit for its designs has long gone to the firm, or to Brinkman, but the Van Nelle company's director and the designer Mart Stam, who worked in the office, both said Van der Vlugt was the creative architect, and the writer Jacob Bakema argued his name should come first.

The Van Nelle Factory in Rotterdam (1931), designed by Van der Vlugt with Mart Stam, is claimed to have the world's first industrially prefabricated curtain wall; Le Corbusier called it "the most beautiful spectacle of the modern age", and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014. The Sonneveld House in Rotterdam (1933) followed, and the Bergpolderflat (1934), a block of flats designed with Willem van Tijen, won international recognition.

facts.claim: Leendert van der Vlugt (13 April 1894 – 25 April 1936), Dutch architect in Rotterdam; in Brinkman & Van der Vlugt responsible for the architecture of the Van Nelle Factory, UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014; after Michiel Brinkman's death in 1925 his son Johannes took over the office with Van der Vlugt as co-director; the office lasted about ten years; Van der Vlugt died in 1936 of Hodgkin's disease

Misleading attribution to Brinkman; quotations from C. H. van der Leeuw and Mart Stam via Jacob Bakema's booklet; Le Corbusier on Van der Vlugt; Bergpolderflat in Rotterdam, 1933–35, with Willem van Tijen, achieved international recognition

Johannes Brinkman, 22 March 1902 – 6 May 1949; exponent of Nieuwe Bouwen; civil engineering at Delft; after 1936 teamed with Johannes Hendrik van den Broek; firm later Van den Broek en Bakema; works: Van Nelle Factory (1931), Sonneveld House (1932)
facts.note: the article dates the Sonneveld House to 1932; the wall gives 1933

facts.claim: Van Nelle Factory: claimed to feature the first industrially prefabricated curtain wall in the world; Le Corbusier (1932): "the most beautiful spectacle of the modern age"; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014

name: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon
bio:
Chamberlin, Powell and Bon was a British architecture firm active above all in the 1950s and 1960s, best known for the Barbican in the City of London and the campus extension of the University of Leeds. It was founded in 1952 by Geoffry Powell (1920–1999), Peter "Joe" Chamberlin (1919–1978) and Christoph Bon (1921–1999), who taught together at Kingston and had agreed that if any of them won the 1951 competition for the Golden Lane Estate they would form a partnership to build it; Powell won. The firm was strongly influenced by Le Corbusier, and many of its works are now listed buildings. Later partners included Charles Greenberg and Frank Woods, and the practice continued until 1989.

The Golden Lane Estate (1962) is valued for a planned landscape that sits between the picturesque and the formal. It led to the commission for the neighbouring Barbican Estate (1982), also for the City of London, a job so large that the firm set up a separate company to handle it. Within it stands the Barbican Centre (1982), a brutalist arts centre with a complex multi-level layout, opened by Queen Elizabeth II.

facts.claim: British firm of architects active in the 1950s and 1960s; best known for the Barbican Estate and the University of Leeds campus extension; founded 1952 by Geoffry Powell (1920–1999), Peter "Joe" Chamberlin (1919–1978) and Christoph Bon (1921–1999) after Powell won the 1951 Golden Lane competition; partners taught at Kingston; agreement to form a partnership if any won

Golden Lane the "apprentice piece"; planned landscape that "straddles the boundary between the picturesque and the formal"; Charles Greenberg partner 1960; Frank Woods; Chamberlin Powell Bon & Woods 1985; continued to 1989; archives at RIBA; influenced by Le Corbusier; many works listed; Barbican so large a sub-practice was set up; Golden Lane Estate 1952–1961
facts.note: the article dates Golden Lane to 1952–1961; the wall gives 1962

facts.claim: Barbican Centre: designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon in the Brutalist style; complex multi-level layout; opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 3 March 1982
